speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you tell me when these symptoms of double vision, difficulty climbing stairs, and upper limb weakness first started, and do they fluctuate throughout the day?

speaker: Patient
text: The double vision usually happens when I look up or down, and the weakness in my arms and legs gets worse after activity but improves if I rest. I have not noticed balance problems or numbness.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you experience any drooping of your eyelids or difficulty swallowing and speaking? Have you noticed if your symptoms worsen later in the day after prolonged activity?

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had recent infections or fevers, and there is no family history of neurological disease. The weakness feels symmetrical in both arms and legs.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the pattern of fluctuating weakness, ptosis, and diplopia worsening with activity, do you have any difficulty swallowing or shortness of breath? I would also like to request specific blood work to check for antibodies. REQUEST TEST: Anti-AChR_Antibodies

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Vital Signs: Temperature 36.6°C (97.9°F), Blood Pressure 125/80 mmHg, Heart Rate 72 bpm, Respiratory Rate 16 breaths/min. Neurological Examination: Presence of ptosis (drooping of the right upper eyelid) worsening with sustained upward gaze; diminished motor strength in upper extremities with normal tone and no atrophy; normal reflexes and sensation throughout. Blood Tests: Acetylcholine Receptor Antibodies Present (elevated). Electromyography: Decreased muscle response with repetitive stimulation. Imaging: Chest CT normal, no thymoma or other masses detected.

speaker: Doctor
text: The clinical picture of fluctuating weakness, ptosis, and elevated acetylcholine receptor antibodies confirms a diagnosis of Myasthenia Gravis. DIAGNOSIS READY: Myasthenia Gravis
